test_title: RRB Technician Grade III Official Paper (Held On: 28 Dec, 2024 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Which of the following statements is true about suspension?

options.text: The solute particles don't settle down when a suspension is left undisturbed.
The particles of a suspension can be seen by the naked eye.
The solute particles cannot be separated from the mixture.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The particles of a suspension can be seen by the naked eye.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles do not dissolve in a liquid solution.
 
• The particles in a suspension are large enough to be seen with the naked eye.
 
• When left undisturbed, the particles in a suspension will eventually settle to the bottom due to gravity.
 
• The particles in a suspension can be separated from the liquid by filtration or decantation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Colloid:**

 
 
• A colloid is a mixture where very small particles of one substance are distributed evenly throughout another substance.
 
• Unlike suspensions, colloids do not settle out upon standing, and the particles cannot be seen with the naked eye.
 
 
 
• **Solution:**
 
 
• A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
 
• The solute is the substance that is dissolved, and the solvent is the substance in which the solute is dissolved.
 
• Solutions are transparent and do not scatter light.
 
 
 
• **Emulsion:**
 
 
• An emulsion is a type of colloid formed by combining two liquids that normally don't mix.
 
• Common examples include milk and mayonnaise.
 
 
 
• **Decantation:**
 
 
• Decantation is a process for the separation of mixtures by removing a liquid layer that is free of precipitate.
 
• This method is commonly used to separate suspensions.
